Florence, February. Pietro has to write a school essay about his family history. In the evening, in the trattoria kitchen, he interviews Grandma Graziella, notebook in hand.
Grandma, for school I have to write about how you met Grandpa Aldo.
Ah… It was 1974. I was twenty and I already worked here, in the trattoria, with my parents.
He was tall, very thin, with hair that was too long. And he had a red bicycle. I had already seen him once, in '66, but I didn't remember him.
One day in March he came into the trattoria, sat down at that table by the window and ordered a ribollita.
Grandma, why are you talking like a book? "Entrò", "si sedette"…
Because that's how old stories are told, sweetheart. If I tell you about yesterday, I say "è entrato". If I tell you about fifty years ago, I say "entrò".
And what did he say to you?
He said: "This ribollita is the best in Florence." And I answered: "I know." He laughed so loudly that the whole trattoria turned round.
And then you got engaged straight away!
Straight away? Not a chance. He came back to eat ribollita every day for a year. Twelve months, before he had the courage to ask me to the cinema.

Pietro worked on the essay for three weeks, every evening, at the kitchen table in the trattoria, while Graziella made dinner and Lupino slept under the chair. First he made the family tree, with the help of Matei, who drew the lines with a ruler as if it were the plan for a restoration. Then he interviewed everyone: Grandma, Dad, Signor Franco, even Bellini. And finally he wrote. The teacher had asked for two pages. Pietro wrote eight.

Signor Franco had been the first to be interviewed. He remembered very well the day Aldo came to Florence to stay, in 1974. "He got off the Bologna train with a cardboard suitcase and the red bicycle," he had said. "I was on duty on platform three. He asked me where via Maggio was. I told him it was a long way, and he answered: 'It doesn't matter, I'll go by bike.' I thought he was mad. I was right: he was mad about your grandmother."

The essay began like this: "My grandfather Aldo died before I was born. I never saw him. But in the last few days I've found out a lot of things, and now I feel as if I know him." Then, to tell the old part, Pietro had decided to use the passato remoto, like Grandma. "That way it sounds like a real book," he had explained to Matei. "And anyway the teacher says that whoever uses the passato remoto always gets a higher mark."

Bellini had agreed to be interviewed too, in his corner of the workshop, with his hands behind his back. He had only known Aldo as an old man, when Aldo used to come into the workshop on Saturdays and sit looking at the paintings, for hours, without saying anything. "I thought he was a curious pensioner," Bellini had said. "I didn't know he had carried my grandfather's Madonna on his shoulders. If I'd known, I'd at least have offered him a coffee."

"My grandfather was born in Bologna in 1948. His father was a printer, and as a boy he too learned to set newspaper pages with lead letters. In November 1966, when the Arno burst its banks, he was eighteen. He took his red bicycle, got on a train to Florence and came to help. He was one of the mud angels."

"In those days he worked with an old restorer, Ernesto Bellini, Professor Bellini's grandfather. Together they saved a Madonna from the church of San Frediano. We know because Ernesto wrote it in his diary, on page forty. But Grandpa never told anyone, not even Grandma. She says that's how he was: he did beautiful things and then forgot about them."

At that point Pietro had made a discovery he hadn't expected. Interviewing Grandma, he had asked her if she had seen Grandpa in 1966. Graziella had said no. Then, one evening, while she was washing up, she had suddenly stopped, a plate in her hand. "Wait," she had said. "Wait a moment." She had sat down, dried her hands on her apron, and told something she had never told anyone.

"In November '66 I was twelve. The trattoria was full of mud up to the windows. My mother was crying, my father was shovelling, and I was hungry, because we hadn't eaten anything hot for two days. One morning a tall young man on a red bicycle covered in dirt went past the door. He stopped, looked at me, opened his rucksack and gave me half a loaf. Then he rode off without a word. I never saw him again. Or at least, that's what I believed for fifty years."

Pietro had stopped writing. "Was it Grandpa?" he had asked. Graziella had smiled, her eyes shining with tears. "I don't know, sweetheart. Maybe. When he came to the trattoria in 1974, he told me my ribollita was the best in Florence, and I thought it was just a compliment. But perhaps… perhaps he had remembered. Perhaps he had come back to see if the little girl with the loaf was all right."

"Then why didn't he tell you?" Graziella shrugged. "Because that's how he was. I told you: he did beautiful things and then forgot about them. Or, more likely, he pretended to forget them, so as not to make anyone feel they owed him." Pietro wrote this in the essay too, word for word, adding in brackets: "(I think he remembered perfectly well.)"

The last part of the essay told of 1974 and 1975: ribollita every day for a year, the first invitation to the cinema after twelve months ("Grandma says he was the shyest boy in Florence"), the wedding at Santo Spirito, the wisteria planted in the garden in 1980, the notches on the nursery door for every one of Dad's birthdays. And the red bicycle, which Matei now uses to get to the workshop, with the basket in front and a tyre that gets a puncture once a month.

Marco, his dad, had added his own memories. Dad standing him against the door frame every birthday, before the cake. Dad whistling while he mended the red bicycle in the courtyard. Dad taking him to the Uffizi on Sundays and saying: "Look carefully, then tell me about it at home." "I thought it was a game," Marco had told his son. "Only now do I understand he was teaching me to look. As he had learned from Ernesto."

The essay ended like this: "I never knew my grandfather. But I know his bicycle, his wisteria, his notches on the door and his big brush, the one Ernesto gave him. And I know Grandma, who still loves him. I think that's enough to know a person. In fact, I'm sure of it."

Pietro read the essay to the class one Monday morning. When he finished, nobody spoke for a few seconds. Then a girl in the front row said: "Miss, can I cry?" The teacher, who was blowing her nose, said yes. The mark was ten out of ten. Underneath, in red pen, the teacher had written: "Excellent use of the passato remoto. But above all, excellent use of the heart."

The next day, half the class asked to see the famous red bicycle. So, on Friday afternoon, Matei brought it to the school, with the basket and the freshly mended tyre. The children looked at it the way you look at a racing car. One asked if he could touch it. Pietro answered, very seriously: "Looking, yes. Touching, no." Then he smiled and added: "All right, just the bell."

That evening Pietro gave the essay to his grandmother. Graziella read it in the kitchen, alone, with her glasses on her nose, twice. Then she went up to her room, opened the drawer where she kept Aldo's things, and put the essay next to the big brush with the blue bristles. "There," she said softly, as if speaking to someone. "Now he knows too."

The following Saturday, at the workshop, Bellini asked Pietro to lend him the essay. He read it in his corner, in silence, his hands trembling a little. Then he took out his black notebook, the new workshop diary, and wrote a line under the date: "Today I read Aldo's story, written by his grandson. My grandfather would be pleased: he too wrote in the passato remoto, and he too, I believe, remembered the little girl with the loaf perfectly well."

Then he closed the notebook, looked towards the trattoria kitchen and asked Graziella, with the utmost seriousness, whether by any chance there was a little ribollita left. Graziella brought it to him in a deep plate, steaming. Bellini tasted it, closed his eyes and said: "It's the best in Florence." Graziella laughed. "I know," she replied. And for a moment, in the trattoria, it felt like 1974.
